section.title: Hosea Redeems Gomer
section.sectionRationale: The shortest chapter is the emotional center of the marriage narrative. God tells Hosea to go and love his adulterous wife again and to buy her back at a price. This costly redemption of an unworthy spouse becomes the clearest picture in the book of the redeeming love of God, and it closes with a promise of Israel seeking the LORD and David their king.
section.thesis: Hosea is commanded to love and redeem his unfaithful wife at real cost, enacting the LORD's love for wayward Israel, and pointing to a future day when a chastened people will return to seek the LORD and their Messianic king.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the command to love her again; the purchase and terms of restoration; and the promise of Israel's return to the LORD and David their king in the last days.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to me, “Go show {{aheb|love}} to your wife again, though she is loved by another and is an adulteress. Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods and love to offer raisin cakes to idols.”
So I {{karah|bought}} her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley.
Then I said to her, “You must live with me for many days; you must not be promiscuous or belong to another, and I will do the same for you.”

units.label: The promise of return
units.note: seeking the LORD and David their king

verses.text: For the Israelites must live many days without king or prince, without sacrifice or sacred pillar, and without ephod or idol.
Afterward, the people of Israel will {{shuv|return}} and seek the LORD their God and David their king. They will come trembling to the LORD and to His goodness in the last days.

aheb.gloss: To love, with warmth and choice. It is used both of Hosea's command to love his straying wife and of the LORD's love for wayward Israel. The same verb even describes Israel loving raisin cakes offered to idols, sharpening the contrast between misplaced human love and God's steadfast, redeeming love.

karah.gloss: To acquire or purchase, here to buy back. Hosea pays a price in silver and barley to reclaim his own wife, who has become another's. The costly buying back pictures redemption, the LORD paying to reclaim a people who had sold themselves into unfaithfulness.

shuv.gloss: To turn, to return, to repent. It is one of Hosea's key words for genuine repentance, a turning back to the LORD. The promise that Israel will return and seek the LORD their God is the hope toward which the whole book strains, fulfilled in true repentance and faith.

basic.context: God tells Hosea to go after his wife again, even though she has been unfaithful and now belongs to another. Hosea has to buy her back, paying silver and barley to reclaim the woman who was already his. Then he sets terms: she is to live faithfully with him. God explains the sign: Israel will go a long time without king, sacrifice, or idol, and then finally turn back to seek the LORD and the coming king in David's line.
basic.hermeneutics: This tiny chapter is deliberately about redemption at a price. The command to love again is stunning precisely because the wife does not deserve it, and that is the point: it mirrors God's love for undeserving Israel. Verse 5 lifts the eyes to the future, a repentant people seeking the LORD and David their king, language the Bible fills out in the Messiah.
basic.originalLanguages: The verb love, aheb, is used four times in verse 1, tying Hosea's love, God's love, and even Israel's misplaced love for idols into one pointed contrast. Hosea buys, karah, his wife back, a picture of redemption. And the promised turning point is shuv, to return or repent, Hosea's great word for coming home to God.
basic.typology: Hosea buying back his adulterous wife foreshadows Christ redeeming His unfaithful people at the cost of His own blood. David their king in verse 5 points beyond David to the promised Son of David, the Messiah, under whom the people will finally return.
basic.christ: The costly purchase of an unworthy bride is fulfilled at the cross, where Christ redeems the church He loves. The promise that Israel will seek David their king in the last days is fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David, to whom repentant people come trembling and find His goodness. He is both the price and the King.
basic.god: We learn that God's love is not a reward for the lovely but a costly commitment to the unfaithful. He does not merely feel love; He pays to reclaim His own. And His discipline, the long years without king or sacrifice, is aimed at producing a genuine, trembling return.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 6:20 says we were bought at a price. Ezekiel 34 and 37 promise one shepherd, David, over God's people. Romans 11 speaks of Israel's future turning to the Lord.
basic.oneStory: Chapter 3 is the marriage narrative's beating heart: love that redeems the undeserving at a price, and a people who will one day return to the LORD and their Davidic king. It points directly to Christ, who buys back His bride and reigns as the Son of David forever.

context.literary:
Hosea 3 is the only chapter of the book in which the prophet speaks in the first person about his own household. Chapter 1 told the story about him in the third person, and chapter 2 was God's speech to the nation. Here Hosea himself says 'the LORD said to me,' 'I bought her,' 'I said to her.' The shift matters, because it lets the reader stand beside the husband at the moment of cost.

The five verses fall into a command, an obedience, a speech to the woman, and an application to Israel. The key is a repeated phrase. In verse 3 the woman is told she must stay with Hosea 'many days,' and in verse 4 the Israelites 'must live many days' without their usual props. In Hebrew it is the same expression, yamim rabbim, and it welds the private and the public sign together. What Gomer endures in her household, Israel will endure in history. The little word 'again' in verse 1 and the 'afterward' that opens verse 5 frame the chapter as a second act and a final one.

The verse that opens the chapter pairs a command with a measure: 'Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites.' The sign is not an arbitrary illustration but a demonstration of how God loves. The chapter's brevity is also its force. Where chapter 1 gave three births and chapter 2 gave twenty three verses of poetry, here almost nothing is said about Gomer's state of mind, the seller, or the setting. All the attention is placed on the price paid and the terms laid down.

Verse 5 forms a bridge into what follows. Chapters 4 to 14 are the long prophetic lawsuit and lament, and its distant hope is the promise stated here, that Israel will return and seek the LORD. Many readers treat the chapter as the hinge between the story of Hosea's family and the message that fills the rest of the book.
context.historical:
The price in verse 2 is given in two forms, silver and grain. Fifteen shekels of silver is about six ounces, as the footnote says, and the barley, a homer and a lethech, was the poor person's staple. Added together, many have reckoned the whole at about the thirty shekels that the law set as compensation for a slave gored by an ox, Exodus 21:32. If that is the intention, Hosea paid the price of a servant. The footnote also records that the Greek reads a homer of barley and a skin of wine, so that the exact form of the payment was not fixed in all the ancient manuscripts.

The situation behind the purchase is not explained. She may have been sold into debt, or kept by a lover, or claimed by a shrine. Debt slavery and the right of a relative to buy back a person were part of Israel's law, Leviticus 25:47-49, and the picture of a man who pays to reclaim what belongs to him would have been familiar to hearers.

The list in verse 4 describes the world Israel treasured. 'King and prince' are the political order, 'sacrifice' and 'ephod' belong to the worship of the LORD, and 'sacred pillar' and household idols belong to the folk religion of the high places. Sacred pillars were forbidden, Deuteronomy 16:22. The ephod, a priestly garment, was misused elsewhere, as when Micah made an ephod and household idols for his private shrine, Judges 17:5. The raisin cakes of verse 1 were festival food, such as David gave to all the people when the ark came to Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 6:19. In idol feasts they became part of an orgy of devotion.

The long period without king, sacrifice and ephod came to pass in the Assyrian conquest, when the last king of Israel was captured and the people were carried away, 2 Kings 17:6. The northern kingdom never again had a king of its own, and Judah too would lose its throne and temple in the Babylonian exile.
context.canonical:
The chapter's last verse links to the promise at the start of the Torah's picture of the end. Moses had said that in distress, 'in later days you will return to the LORD your God and listen to His voice,' Deuteronomy 4:30. Hosea 3:5 uses the same expression for the days that lie beyond the judgment. The phrase 'in the last days' has the same sound as Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49:1 and becomes a regular marker of the prophets' vision of the end.

The expectation of David as the future king is echoed by Jeremiah, 'they will serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them,' Jeremiah 30:9, and by Ezekiel's picture of a shepherd David in Ezekiel 34:23-24. Amos closes his book with the promise of the restoration of the fallen tent of David, Amos 9:11, and James quotes it in Acts 15:16 when the council considers the Gentiles. In the New Testament the angel announces to Mary that the Lord God will give her son 'the throne of His father David,' Luke 1:32-33.

The redemption image is also taken up across Scripture. Hosea himself returns to it when he writes of ransom from Sheol and redemption from death, Hosea 13:14, a line Paul reshapes in the argument of 1 Corinthians 15. The New Testament says that believers were 'bought at a price,' 1 Corinthians 6:20, and redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. Jesus Himself says the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Hosea wanted the hearers to see that the story of Gomer did not end at the courtroom of chapter 2. The command is a second demonstration, this time of what God's love costs and what it requires. He wanted them to hear that the price was paid by the one who had been wronged. Nothing in the chapter suggests that Gomer arranged her own return or that she deserved the effort.

He also wanted them to understand the long silence. The terms laid down in verse 3 are not a punishment for its own sake but a period in which the old loyalties are cut off, so that a restored relationship has room to grow. Israel's exile would be a time of absence, with no king, no worship system and no idols, and the hearer is told in advance that this is part of the love and not its failure.

Finally, he gave the people something to look toward. 'Afterward' is the pivot of the whole prophecy. After the many days there would be a seeking, a trembling and a goodness. The hearers could face the coming disaster as a loss that had a purpose and an end, held in the hand of the one who had already shown that He would buy back what He loved.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records a single act by a single prophet. It does not tell husbands to buy back their wives or to remarry them after adultery, and it is not a rule about divorce. Jeremiah 3:1 shows that Israel's law had its own hard questions about return after a second marriage, and Hosea 3 does not remove them for ordinary households. The text does not describe the legal details of the transaction, which is a sign that the legal detail is not its point.

What the passage prescribes is the shape of love. It teaches that the love of God does not wait for the one loved to become lovable, and that those who bear His name are to love 'as the LORD loves,' which means in costly ways to people who have not earned it. It also provides a pattern for how God deals with His people when they have wandered: He sets terms that cut off the old attachments and holds out the promise of a return. For the church, that means discipline and waiting need not be read as abandonment, and that the promise of verse 5 is held for a people who will come 'trembling' to the LORD's goodness.

debates.question: Is the woman of verse 1 Gomer, or another woman?

views.label: Gomer, taken back
views.case: The command to love 'your wife again' most naturally refers to the wife of chapter 1, and the word 'again' fits a repeat of Hosea's earlier love. The plain sequence, in which a husband buys back a wife who has gone to another, makes the sign of redemption sharper.

views.label: A second woman
views.case: The woman is not named here, and the Hebrew can be read 'a woman loved by a companion,' as the footnote shows. Some see a different woman who stands for the same message. They note that the sign, not the name, carries the point.

debates.bearing: The meaning is the same either way, since the sign is about how the LORD loves an adulterous people. The simpler reading, that this is Gomer, fits the structure of the marriage story best.

debates.question: What do the terms of verse 3 mean for Gomer?

views.label: A period of abstinence
views.case: The phrase 'I will do the same for you' is taken to mean that Hosea too will keep from relations during the time, a season of separation within the household that matches Israel's years without its usual worship.

views.label: A pledge of mutual faithfulness
views.case: Others read the sentence as a promise that the husband will be wholly faithful to her, so the many days are a time of settled, exclusive devotion and not a sentence of distance.

debates.bearing: The text is brief and the grammar open, so the safest course is to hold to what is clear: the period is a time of restraint that prepares for restoration.

debates.question: Does 'the last days' refer to the return from exile or to the age of the Messiah?

views.label: A return in the near future
views.case: Hosea's own hearers would see in it the end of the exile and the reunion of the people with David's throne, as in Jeremiah 30:9.

views.label: The age begun in Christ
views.case: The New Testament takes 'the last days' as the time inaugurated by Jesus, Acts 2:36, so that seeking David their king is fulfilled when people come to Jesus, the Son of David.

debates.bearing: Both readings may be held together, since the prophets look past the return to a larger fulfilment, and the New Testament shows that it has begun in Christ and awaits completion.

study.originalLanguages:
The command in verse 1 is compressed. The Hebrew says she is loved by a re'a, a friend or companion, and is an adulteress, menaefet, a participle describing a continuing state. The footnote offers a different arrangement, 'a woman who is loved by another,' because the Hebrew is compressed. Either way the sentence presents love as aimed at someone who is currently loved by another and is guilty.

The repetition of the verb love is the key to the verse. It gives the command, 'show love,' then names the woman as 'loved' by another, then sets the standard in the 'love' of the LORD, and ends with the love of the nation for 'raisin cakes.' The footnote on that last phrase says it literally reads 'and love raisin cakes.' Raisin cakes were festival food, as 2 Samuel 6:19 and Song of Songs 2:5 show, and here they stand for the cult meals offered to the idols. The people prefer the festival of a false god to the God of the festival.

Verse 2 says 'I bought her,' and the Hebrew adds a small word meaning 'for myself,' so that he buys her to be his own. The price is stated twice, in silver and in grain, and the footnote on the barley notes that another reading counts a homer and a half, and that the Greek differs. Hosea does not use the ordinary word for redeem, ga'al, in this chapter, though he will use it in 13:14. The point of the chapter is the transaction, a payment made.

Verse 3 repeats the phrase yamim rabbim, 'many days,' and in the same breath gives three negatives for the woman: she is to stay, not to be promiscuous, and not to be for another man. The verb for 'live' means to sit or dwell, and it often implies waiting, so that she is to remain in a settled, quiet place. The final clause, 'and I also toward you,' is left without a verb in the Hebrew, which is why translators fill in 'I will do the same for you.'

The list in verse 4 is balanced in pairs. 'King' and 'prince' are the civil order. 'Sacrifice' and 'sacred pillar' pair legitimate offering with an illegitimate standing stone. 'Ephod' and the last word, teraphim, which the BSB renders 'idol,' pair a priestly garment with household images. The loss includes what was commanded and what was forbidden, so that Israel is left with neither.

In verse 5 the verb shuv, return, is joined with baqqesh, seek, and with 'they will come trembling,' from the root pachad, which means to be in awe or fear. The nation comes to 'the LORD and to His goodness,' tuvo, a word for the whole good that He gives. The phrase 'in the last days' is literally 'in the end of the days.'

typology.fulfillment: A husband pays a price in silver and barley to buy back a wife who has given herself to another. The pattern is redemption at cost. It is fulfilled in Christ, who gave 'His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, and in whose blood believers are redeemed, not with 'silver or gold' but with the blood of a lamb without blemish, 1 Peter 1:18-19. Paul says, 'you were bought at a price,' 1 Corinthians 6:20. The correspondence is complete in the shape of the act but the type falls short in the price: Hosea paid the value of a slave, and Christ paid with His own life.

If the whole sum approximates the thirty shekels due for a slave, Exodus 21:32, it prefigures how little the world valued the Redeemer. The chief priests set thirty pieces of silver on Jesus, Matthew 26:15, and Matthew sees Zechariah's 'magnificent price' fulfilled in it, Matthew 27:3-9. The irony is the same in both: the one who pays the price of a slave to free the unworthy is himself valued at a slave's price. The correspondence is suggestive, not certain, since the total in Hosea is a calculation by readers and not a statement of the text.

The season of restraint in Gomer's house and the long period of Israel's exile without king, sacrifice or idol are linked by the same phrase. It points to a time of preparation before restoration. In the New Testament, Paul writes of a hardening in part that has come to Israel 'until the full number of the Gentiles has come in,' Romans 11:25-26, and so the many days continue to be a time God uses. The type falls short because it describes a season of national history, and the New Testament sees a larger plan that includes the nations.

The nation that once cried 'What portion do we have in David?' in 1 Kings 12:16 will seek David their king. David is the pattern of a shepherd king, and the promise is that a ruler like him will gather the scattered. The angel tells Mary that her son will receive 'the throne of His father David,' Luke 1:32-33. The type falls short because David was a sinful king whose house failed, while the Son of David reigns forever and His kingdom will never end.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by the shape of redemption. The husband in Hosea 3 pays a price for someone who cannot pay it herself and who has given herself to another. The gospel is exactly that. Jesus says He came 'to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10, and that He would give His life as a ransom, Mark 10:45. Peter tells the church that the cost was not silver or gold but the blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The chapter's quiet insistence that the money is paid before any change in the bride is the same as the claim that 'while we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8.

It leads to Christ by the kingly promise of verse 5. The nation will seek 'the LORD their God and David their king.' In the Old Testament this is a way of saying that the Davidic line will be restored. The New Testament announces that the line has come to its goal in Jesus, whom God has made 'both Lord and Christ,' Acts 2:36. The people who come to Him do so, as verse 5 says, 'trembling,' in fear and in hope, and find 'His goodness.' The Son of David both fulfils the kingly promise and provides the redemption price.

It leads to Christ by the pattern of the cost to the redeemer. Hosea is told to love someone who is loved by another. The Son of God loves a people who have given themselves to other loves, and He does not wait for them to change before acting. The apostle puts it in terms of the law: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13, so that 'we might receive our adoption as sons,' Galatians 4:5. The price in Hosea buys back a wife, and the price in Christ buys back a people who become sons and a bride.

It leads to Christ by the possible echo of the price. If the sum in Hosea is a slave's price, the sale of Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, Matthew 26:15, has a terrible irony. The one who paid the price of a slave to free the guilty was Himself priced as a slave by those He came to free.

The chapter needs a guard against over reading. The details of the raisin cakes, the homer and the lethech do not each hide a symbol. What the apostles take is the act of redemption at cost, and the hope of a king from David's line to whom the people return.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God whose love begins before the beloved responds. The command to Hosea sets a standard: 'Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods.' The love of God is described with the very condition that would make human love withdraw. He loves a people who are already given to another and who still love the festival foods of an idol. The text does not say that He loves them because they are lovable. It says He loves them.

He is a God who pays. Verse 2 pictures the cost with an almost bookkeeping precision: so much silver, so much barley. God does not simply cancel the debt of Israel's betrayal. He takes it upon Himself. The cost of mercy in Hosea is the outer edge of a theme that finds its fullest expression in the cross, and later prophets say it with more force, as in Isaiah 53:6, where the LORD lays on His servant 'the iniquity of us all.'

He is a God who sets terms. Love in this chapter is not indulgence. Hosea tells the woman she must stay, must not give herself to another, and he will keep faith with her. God's love for His people includes a call to be His alone, and His discipline is part of the covenant. The many days without king, sacrifice or idol are not a sign that He has given up but that He is clearing away everything that stood between them.

He is also a God who keeps time. The chapter looks to 'afterward' and to 'the last days,' and holds that history is moving toward a return. He does not forget that He promised a king from David. The same hand that allows the kingdom to be stripped will raise up the king, and the same love that sends exile will bring people home. His anger is real but not final, as Hosea 14:4 says: 'I will heal their apostasy; I will freely love them, for My anger has turned away from them.'

For worship, the chapter calls us to let the price paid shape our praise. We love because we have been bought, and we are called to hold ourselves for Him. It also teaches patience in seasons of waiting, since a long silence may be the space in which He is preparing a return.

crossReferences.note: The command to take a wife and her marriage to Gomer. Chapter 3 begins with the word 'again' because it repeats and deepens that sign, now with the added cost of redemption. The two accounts together frame the prophet's household as a message.
The compensation for a servant gored by an ox is thirty shekels of silver. The total in Hosea 3:2 may come near that figure, which would present Gomer as bought at the price of a slave.

A relative may redeem a countryman who has sold himself into debt. Hosea acts as the near kinsman for his own wife, paying to recover someone who has lost her freedom, and the law gives the picture of redemption its legal background.

Micah makes an ephod and household idols for his private shrine. It explains the pairing of 'ephod' and 'idol' in Hosea 3:4 and shows how the priestly garment had been dragged into the folk religion Hosea condemns.

The northern tribes broke from the house of David with the cry 'What portion do we have in David?' Hosea 3:5 promises that the same people will one day seek 'David their king,' reversing the break that formed the northern kingdom.

Moses says that in distress, 'in later days you will return to the LORD your God.' It is the earlier statement of the hope in Hosea 3:5, and shows that the return after judgment was part of the covenant from the start.

The people will serve the LORD and 'David their king, whom I will raise up for them.' Jeremiah repeats Hosea's phrase and shows that the promise of a Davidic king was a settled hope of the prophets after Hosea.

The LORD says He will ransom from the power of Sheol and redeem from Death. It extends the redemption of Hosea 3 from the household to the grave, showing that the bought-back wife stands for a people rescued from death.

Believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ. It takes the idea of cost in Hosea 3:2 and sets the true price beside it, showing that the silver was only a picture of a greater payment.

The chief priests weigh out thirty pieces of silver for Jesus. If Hosea's sum approximates a slave's price, it makes a poignant parallel: the Redeemer is valued at the rate of the servant He came to free.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story has an obvious problem in its middle: how can a holy God keep a people who keep leaving Him? Hosea 3 gives the answer in a single act. He pays. The garden story ended with exile and with a promise of a seed, and the long story of Israel shows how deep the need is. Chapter 3 compresses it into a marriage, a price and a long wait.

Looking back, the chapter draws on the Torah's law of redemption, in which a kinsman could buy back a relative who had lost freedom, and on the exodus, where God redeemed a people from slavery with a strong arm. Israel's story begins with a purchase, Exodus 15:16, and Hosea reminds the nation that the buying is not over. The chapter also draws on Moses' warning that distress would come and on his promise that in later days the people would return, Deuteronomy 4:30.

Looking forward, the chapter points to the exile and the silence that followed. The northern kingdom was carried off by Assyria and did not have a king again, and Judah lost its throne and temple to Babylon. In those years, the many days passed. The prophets spoke of a return, and a remnant came back, but the promised king did not yet reign. The New Testament opens with the announcement that the king has come, Luke 1:32-33, and that the redemption price has been paid, Mark 10:45.

The story ends in a new creation where the bride has been bought and made ready. Revelation 5:9 shows the song of the redeemed: 'You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.' The purchase that Hosea made for one wife is made for a multitude, and the many days of waiting come to an end when the king comes. Those who had been told 'not My people' are His own, and the price that was paid is celebrated forever.

quiz.q: What made God's command to Hosea in verse 1 so striking?

options.text: He was to love and reclaim a wife who was unfaithful and now belonged to another, as a picture of God's love for Israel.
options.note: Verse 1 explicitly links Hosea's love to the LORD's love for a people who turn to other gods.

options.text: He was told to find a new and better wife.
options.note: The point is reclaiming the same fallen wife, not replacing her.

options.text: He was to divorce her permanently.
options.note: The command is to love and restore, the opposite of divorce.

options.text: He was told to love her only if she changed first.
options.note: The love comes toward her while she is still unfaithful, not as a reward.

quiz.q: What is the significance of Hosea buying his wife back?

options.text: It pictures redemption, paying a price to reclaim someone who had become enslaved to unfaithfulness.
options.note: The price roughly equals that of a slave, foreshadowing being bought at a price.

options.text: It shows that love is mainly a financial transaction.
options.note: The payment dramatizes costly love, not a mercenary view of relationships.

options.text: It proves Gomer was worth the investment.
options.note: The point is grace toward the unworthy, not her worthiness.

options.text: It was an ordinary marriage custom with no deeper meaning.
options.note: The purchase is a deliberate sign of redemption.

quiz.q: What does the long period without king, sacrifice, or idol in verse 4 represent?

options.text: A season of stripping and waiting meant to bring Israel to a genuine return to God.
options.note: The deprivation parallels the terms Hosea set for Gomer, aimed at restoration.

options.text: God's final and permanent abandonment of Israel.
options.note: Verse 5 shows the waiting ends in return, not abandonment.

options.text: A time of great prosperity and freedom.
options.note: It is a time of loss and discipline, not prosperity.

options.text: Proof that worship no longer matters to God.
options.note: The aim is renewed true worship of the LORD.

quiz.q: Who is David their king in verse 5?

options.text: The promised Son of David, the Messiah fulfilled in Jesus, to whom the people return.
options.note: David was long dead; the prophecy looks to the Messianic king in David's line.

options.text: King David risen from the dead to rule again personally.
options.note: It points to David's greater Son, not David himself returning.

options.text: Any future political leader of Israel.
options.note: It specifically anticipates the Davidic Messiah, not just any ruler.

options.text: A symbol with no real fulfillment.
options.note: The New Testament shows it fulfilled in Christ, the Son of David.

quiz.q: What does this chapter reveal about God's love?

options.text: It is costly, freely given to the undeserving, and aimed at bringing His people home.
options.note: Redeeming love toward the unfaithful is the chapter's central revelation.

options.text: It is given only to those who earn it.
options.note: The love here reaches the unfaithful before they change, not as earned reward.

options.text: It is mostly words with no real action or cost.
options.note: The love is enacted at real cost, in silver and barley and commitment.

options.text: It eventually gives up on unfaithful people.
options.note: The chapter shows love that reclaims rather than abandons.

questions: God told Hosea to love his wife again while she was still unfaithful. How does it affect you to know that God loved you before you were lovely or willing?
Hosea paid a real price to reclaim his wife. What does it mean to you that Christ bought you back at the cost of His own blood?
Israel had to endure a long, stripped-down season before returning to God. Is there a barren stretch in your life that God may be using to draw you home?
The chapter promises a people who come trembling to the LORD and to His goodness. What would it look like for reverence and joy in God's goodness to grow together in you?
Repentance in Hosea is a returning, shuv. Is there an area where the Lord is inviting you to turn back to Him today?

translationNotes.note: An alternate rendering is Go show love to a woman who is loved by another; the flow of the marriage narrative favors reference to Gomer. The clause love raisin cakes reflects a literal Hebrew idiom for delighting in idol feasts.
Fifteen shekels of silver is about six ounces or 171 grams; a homer and a lethech of barley is roughly a homer and a half, together approximating the price of a slave.
David their king refers to the promised ruler in David's line, the Messiah, rather than David personally, as David had long since died.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Hosea 3:1-5.
